clue.text: Accumulating money, darling, is a redeeming feature!

parts.note: putting money by is saving
Grace Darling was the Victorian lighthouse keeper's daughter famed for a sea rescue, so the surname calls up her first name

explanation.surface: Someone praises a thrifty sweetheart, whose penny-pinching is the one thing that redeems them.
explanation.walkthrough: Grace Darling (1815-42) rowed out with her father to rescue shipwrecked sailors off the Northumberland coast; the clue gives her surname to point to her first name.
explanation.definitionFit: A quality that makes up for someone's other faults is the one thing that rescues their character.

clue.text: Unhappy, I take to the streets, finding cruel people

parts.note: unhappy means sad
ST is the abbreviation for street, so streets are STS

explanation.surface: A miserable protester takes to the streets and meets only cruelty.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who take pleasure in inflicting pain on others are the cruellest of people.

clue.text: One view taken of violet's soldiers

indicators.note: the letter for one is taken into the middle of the abbreviation for violet's

parts.note: V stands for violet, as in the rainbow's colour initials, and the possessive adds S
the Roman numeral for one is I
the TA, the Territorial Army, is Britain's volunteer reserve of soldiers

explanation.surface: A painter considers one scene showing a regiment in purple uniforms.
explanation.walkthrough: The TA (Territorial Army) is the British part-time army reserve, a crossword staple for soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: A vista is a broad scenic prospect, a sweeping outlook over the landscape.

clue.text: Zen (sic) the basis for this philosopher

indicators.note: these letters are the raw material on which the name is built by rearrangement

explanation.surface: A note insists that Zen, spelt just so, underlies the thinking of a certain philosopher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'basis for' signals an anagram: the nine letters of ZEN SIC THE rearrange into the German thinker's surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Friedrich Nietzsche was the nineteenth-century German thinker behind Thus Spoke Zarathustra.

clue.text: Brag about a seizure

indicators.note: about here means moved around, so the letters of brag are shuffled into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone boasts about a snatch they made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' tells you to rearrange the letters of BRAG.
explanation.definitionFit: A grab is a sudden snatching or taking hold of something.

clue.text: Spray a Tom is putting on first two ericas

indicators.note: putting on means adding the following letters at the end
first two asks for the opening pair of letters of the word ericas

explanation.surface: A cat named Tom puts on a spray of heather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first two' takes ER from 'ericas', and 'putting on' adds it to A TOM IS. Ericas are heathers.
explanation.definitionFit: An atomiser is a device that turns liquid such as perfume into a fine mist.

clue.text: Each year always comes before

indicators.note: comes before puts the word for always ahead of the year abbreviation

parts.note: always means ever, as in ever hopeful

explanation.surface: Each year it always arrives before its time.
explanation.definitionFit: Every and each both pick out all members of a group taken one at a time.

clue.text: Money that is used at a club

parts.note: brass is British slang for money
i.e. abbreviates id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: Cash is what gets used at a members' club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brass' is northern English slang for money. The surface suggests a nightclub, but the club is for golf.
explanation.definitionFit: A brassie is an old name for a golf wood, the number two, once soled with brass.

clue.text: Determined to start, to capture law-breaker

indicators.note: the word start captures the rearranged letters inside it
a breaker smashes things, so the word law is broken up and its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A determined police force sets out to catch a criminal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'law-breaker' splits: 'breaker' signals an anagram of LAW, giving LWA, which 'to capture' puts inside START.
explanation.definitionFit: A stalwart supporter is staunch and resolute, firmly loyal.

clue.text: Ruffian inviting o'Connor for a party

parts.note: Des O'Connor was a British television entertainer and singer
per means for each, as in per head
a do is a party or celebration

explanation.surface: A thug sends an invitation to a famous entertainer for a party.
explanation.walkthrough: Des O'Connor (1932-2020) was a long-running British TV host and crooner.
explanation.definitionFit: A desperado is a reckless outlaw, a bold and dangerous criminal of the Wild West kind.

clue.text: Former artwork is additional

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife

indicators.note: work here means to work over, so the letters of art are reshaped

explanation.surface: A gallery-goer finds that an old painting is an extra one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'artwork' splits: 'work' signals an anagram of ART, giving TRA.
explanation.definitionFit: Something extra is supplementary, more than is usual or expected.

clue.text: The way a new Zealand amateur creates verse

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: A New Zealand hobbyist poet writes verse in their own way.
explanation.definitionFit: A stanza is a group of lines forming a unit of a poem.

clue.text: Told to buy reaping equipment, in exchange for vehicles

indicators.note: told means spoken, so the phrase is heard rather than read

parts.note: to buy reaping equipment is to buy sickles, the curved blades for cutting crops

explanation.surface: A farmer is told to purchase harvesting gear in exchange for vehicles.
explanation.walkthrough: BUY SICKLES, spoken, sounds like the two-wheelers.
explanation.definitionFit: Bicycles are pedal-driven two-wheelers, a form of transport.

clue.text: A smart-looking tree?

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a tree could be called well dressed.
explanation.definitionFit: Spruce means neat and trim in appearance; a spruce is also a conifer, such as the Norway species used for Christmas.

clue.text: Renew damaged tree the star put in

indicators.note: the star is put in among the rearranged letters
damaged means the letters of tree are knocked out of order

parts.note: a nova is a star that suddenly brightens

explanation.surface: To restore a damaged tree, someone puts the star back on top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'damaged' rearranges TREE into RETE, and 'put in' sets NOVA inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To renovate is to restore something to good condition, making it like new again.

clue.text: Diffuse, as mate pre-arranged with last bottle

indicators.note: arranged means the letters of mate and pre are put in a new order
last asks for the final letter of the word bottle

explanation.surface: A friend set up in advance spreads out, with the last bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pre-arranged' splits: 'arranged' signals an anagram of MATE and PRE; 'last bottle' adds E.
explanation.definitionFit: To permeate is to spread through and pervade something throughout.

clue.text: Begging for a fix? I'm unable to finish

indicators.note: to finish puts the phrase for being unable at the end

parts.note: to mend something is to fix it
I'm unable means I can't

explanation.surface: Someone begs for a repair but can't complete the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to finish' places I CANT after MEND. The surface's 'fix' suggests a drug.
explanation.definitionFit: Mendicant describes living by alms, as do certain orders of friars.

clue.text: Sweet paste — get sick swallowing it? On the contrary!

indicators.note: swallowing it says one word goes inside the other
on the contrary reverses who swallows whom, so paste swallows sick

parts.note: taken as written
ill means sick

explanation.surface: A child eats sweet paste and asks whether it will make them ill.
explanation.walkthrough: As written, 'sick swallowing it' puts PASTE inside ILL; 'On the contrary' flips that, putting ILL inside PASTE.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastille is a small chewable sweet or lozenge.

clue.text: Old man Joyce entitled to his wake?

definitions.text: Old man Joyce entitled to his wake?

parts.words: Old man Joyce entitled to his wake?
parts.note: Joyce's last novel names a wake after an Irishman, so the old man in the title is the one whose wake it is

explanation.surface: An elderly man named Joyce asks whether he has earned a funeral gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: James Joyce's novel Finnegans Wake takes its title from a ballad about a man who revives at his own wake.
explanation.definitionFit: Tim Finnegan is the hod-carrier of the Irish ballad and Joyce's title, the dead man at the wake.

clue.text: Completes form and acts as locum

explanation.surface: A stand-in doctor also does the paperwork.
explanation.definitionFit: To complete a form is to write in the blanks; to stand in for an absent colleague is to deputise.

clue.text: Sneak taking cans back for heating

indicators.note: back means the word for cans is read in reverse

parts.note: cans are tins
CH is the abbreviation for central heating

explanation.surface: A thief takes tin cans away to use as fuel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns TINS into SNIT. CH is a common estate-agent abbreviation for central heating.
explanation.definitionFit: A snitch is an informer, someone who tells tales on others.

clue.text: The number reached by old division

explanation.surface: A total is arrived at by an ancient sum.
explanation.walkthrough: In England a hundred was an old subdivision of a county.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the figure ten times ten; the other is a historic administrative area within an English shire.

clue.text: Lift Jacob's son gets to the gallery

parts.note: Levi was one of the twelve sons of Jacob in Genesis
the Tate is the London art gallery

explanation.surface: A son of Jacob takes the lift up to the gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is a group of major British art galleries, including Tate Modern in London.
explanation.definitionFit: To levitate is to rise or raise into the air, apparently defying gravity.

clue.text: Give more drink to the little dog?

parts.note: taken as written
a pup is a young dog

explanation.surface: Someone asks if the puppy should be given a refill.
explanation.definitionFit: To top up is to refill someone's glass before it is empty.

clue.text: A bit of tennis? Sensible to hold it in the hut

indicators.note: a bit of means the answer is only part of these words
to hold it says the words contain the answer within them

explanation.surface: A player wonders whether it is sensible to hold a bit of tennis in a hut.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'tenNIS SENsible'. A Nissen hut is a prefabricated corrugated-iron shelter.
explanation.definitionFit: A Nissen is a half-cylinder corrugated-iron shelter, used widely as military housing.

clue.text: What a chair may be called in France

definitions.text: What a chair may be called in France

parts.words: What a chair may be called in France
parts.note: a carried chair is named after a French town, so the clue reads as a French name for a chair

explanation.surface: Someone asks what the French word for chair is.
explanation.walkthrough: A sedan chair was an enclosed seat carried on poles; Sedan is also a town in north-east France.
explanation.definitionFit: A sedan is an enclosed seat borne on poles, and also a French town on the Meuse.

clue.text: Time we English became small and pretty!

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: In time, we English became dainty and sweet.
explanation.definitionFit: Twee describes something excessively dainty or quaint, cute to the point of sentimentality.

clue.text: Is put back, to become alert

indicators.note: back means each of the two little words is read in reverse in its own place

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something is replaced, so people start paying attention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns both words round where they stand: IS becomes SI and PUT becomes TUP.
explanation.definitionFit: To sit up is to take notice suddenly, as in 'that made them sit up'.

clue.text: He doesn't enjoy the high life in Scotland

definitions.text: He doesn't enjoy the high life in Scotland

parts.words: He doesn't enjoy the high life in Scotland
parts.note: the high life suggests luxury, but here it is life in the mountainous north of Scotland

explanation.surface: A Scotsman shuns glamour and luxury.
explanation.walkthrough: Scotland divides into Highlands and Lowlands; someone from the southern part does not live the Highland life.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of the southern, flatter part of Scotland, as opposed to a Highlander.

clue.text: Doomed to be a nuisance, including a colourful description that takes in journalist

indicators.note: including means the nuisance holds the colour word inside it

parts.note: a pest is a nuisance
red describes a colour
taken as written
ED, short for editor, is the usual crossword journalist

explanation.surface: Someone fated to be an irritant is caught in a vivid write-up by a reporter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'including' puts RED inside PEST to make PREDEST; IN and ED follow, with 'that takes' only joining.
explanation.definitionFit: Predestined means fated in advance, settled by destiny beforehand.
